utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We understand there is a matter to be raised by the Prosecution and a matter to be raised by the Defence. Are they the same matter? It seems that they may be the same matter. This is the question of exhibits for the next witness. Do you want to have first go, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I don't like starting our working week with an objection, but I have to. I don't know whether Mr. Stamp should go first in terms of introduction and then respond to our objection. In any case, it may not be relevant. We wanted to raise an issue which would be raised in any case eventually during the day. I'll start by drawing a broad picture which has to do with the use of certain witnesses as expert witnesses in a broad sense of the word. By this I mean that these people were in certain positions at the relevant time and then they are asked to offer their comments and interpretations of certain things, which as fact witnesses they would not be able to. On the other hand, they frequently discuss matters that can only be weighed by the Bench itself and used in the judgement. What is interesting in terms of the next witness is that he was retired between 1992 and 1999. He was reinstated and in one part of the relevant period for this indictment he was in active duty and was an eye-witness. We know of the position that certain witnesses, due to their tasks at the time, can provide us with significant assistance. I am against such witnesses being used as expert witnesses, though. Namely, Defence believes that one needs to prepare differently when one needs to hear an expert witness pursuant to Rule 94, I believe; and it is another matter when we hear fact witnesses be live or pursuant to 92 ter. When it comes to witnesses, Defence comes up with its own witness, analyses the documents commented upon by the witness of the other party. We know what their opinion is, we know what their finding is, and then we argue facts. And it is up to the Bench to see whether their witness testimony is viable or not. With fact witnesses used as expert witnesses, this becomes far more difficult to do. Now to go back to the issue of proposed exhibits and the expansion of the 65 ter list. Defence received from the Prosecution a request to amend their 65 ter list which was on Friday, the 5th of June, this year after 5.00 p.m., after office hours. In that request, the Prosecutor seeks to amend and add items to the 65 ter list by means of nine new exhibits or documents. On Sunday, the 7th of June of this year, at 6.00 p.m., the Prosecutor contacted Defence with a filing which was a corrigendum or an addendum to their filing of the 5th of June, stating that by mistake an additional eight documents were omitted. In both these filings the Prosecutor seeks to expand its 65 ter list by these new 17 documents. This fact alone, that is to say that we have quite a large number of documents, poses a problem for the Defence given the resources that we have. Another issue is that all of those 17 documents is something that the Prosecutor envisaged to use during this witness's testimony today. The reasons that the Prosecutor states for which they seek to add these documents are as follows. One of them is omission, oversight. These documents are of great importance for these proceedings. Defence believes that this was no oversight on the part of the OTP or that these are not important documents for the following reasons. Today's witness has been on the 65 ter list of the OTP as of 1 September 2008. As of that time, there was an initial list of documents pursuant to 65 ter that the Prosecutor had planned to use. We believe that that 65 ter list, which was forwarded at that stage, enabled both the Chamber and Defence to prepare themselves given the scope, the volume, of the documents to be studied and prepared. After 1 September 1998 [sic] the Prosecutor submitted on the 14th of January a request that this witness be heard under Rule 92 ter; having in mind this proposal, the Prosecutor at that time put forth some exhibits and documents that were to be used during that witness's testimony. They stated the documents they intended to use. In that submission, we find none of the 17 documents they are seeking to introduce now. I would particularly like to point out that Defence is aware of the technical problems that the OTP may run into, particularly since we will face the same problems once our case begins and that none of the dead-lines are set in stone and that one needs to interpret those flexibly. However, we received the Prosecutor's report on the 25th of May, 2009, stating that this witness will be heard this week. He was the first person on the list for the week. In the course of the past 11 days, the Prosecutor did not notify Defence of their wish to expand the 65 ter list with the documents to be used -- put through to this witness. They did so for the first time last Friday and then yesterday afternoon. I would like to state that this witness testified twice before this Tribunal in the Milosevic case and the Milutinovic case, and that we find it strange that after such two cases they only discover relevant documents now, some relevant documents that should be admitted through this witness here today. I would like to tell the Chamber that some, perhaps most of these documents, were disclosed to Defence at the end of last week. And some, although disclosed earlier, were not marked as documents to be heard during the testimony of this witness, it was pursuant to our request. Several other Chambers from other proceedings ordered that these documents be disclosed to us. We believed that we might find some of those documents useful during our case. That disclosure was not done for the sake of the Prosecutor, and in the 65 ter list of the OTP we now find some of such documents as I have already stated. In addition to the request to expand the list with the 17 documents, we simultaneously received a set of documents under Rule 66. All those documents, if we put them together, have over 1.000 pages. Defence was physically unable to even leaf through those documents, so as to be able to prepare within this very short period. Your Honours, I believe that there are no justified reasons to accept this 65 ter list expansion with the 17 documents put forth by the Prosecutor. Defence also wanted to tell you that in all likelihood those documents are relevant for this case, as all of the documents we have used so far were. I don't think there was a single document that was irrelevant for the proceedings. Still, one has to raise the issue of criteria of admission in this case and whether some documents - although I may be skipping ahead -- and if all documents can be introduced through any which witness. One such witness was shown a document signed by a person whose signature he could recognise. For example, I'm now quite familiar with Mr. Stamp's signature by now. Does that mean that I can testify to the veracity of his signature and whether that document could be admitted solely on that basis? That is why I believe that this Bench, in keeping with its earlier decisions, should try to regulate or channel the principle used when admitting documents; and to reiterate our request, we seek that the Prosecutor not be allowed to expand their 65 ter list with those 17 documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I think I should start by agreeing and accepting what my friend said, that these documents are clearly relevant and probative to the issues before the Court. I also concede, as in the -- as indicated in the filing, that these documents were missed by oversight. I -- looking at the numbers, I see that it is likely that many or most of them were documents that were brought by various of the Defence teams in the Milutinovic case. And I also agree with counsel that when we are handing such a huge mass of material in cases of this nature that oversights will occur, and he did concede that he expected that when his time comes there will be such oversights with documents, although I'm not sure I would take the same position as he normally takes when these things occur. That being said, Your Honour, I wish to submit that the primary consideration is whether or not the prejudice to the Defence is undue and cannot be remedied. The Prosecution sought to add these documents at this time because this is a witness who can identify them, and the Prosecution at this stage will not be asking the witness to discuss the contents of these documents. However, it is also mentioned that the countervailing issue is whether or not a witness who is here who can comment on documents which both parties accept and agree are relevant to the issues before the Chamber, whether he should be allowed to comment on these documents or to at least identify them or if we should just allow him to leave without being given the opportunity. I also seek to mention and I mention that this is an application to just expand the list so that he could be shown these documents and comment on it -- on them. And depending on whether or not in the course of time when the witness is in The Hague - and we could ask him if he will remain here for a day or two more - the Defence could consider over that period of time whether or not these additional documents would prejudice them in terms of their preparation and if they would have additional questions for that witness. So although I -- there are many areas where I agree with counsel, especially as regards relevance and probative value of the documents and the fact that -- and this is not an excuse, it is just a reality that sometimes these things happen in respect to managing so many documents - I think the Court should consider the balance of prejudice and whether it is irremediable. And I think we, the Prosecution, can take steps to accommodate the Defence if they have problems reviewing these 17 documents to give them an opportunity to do whatever preparations they might want to address these documents with the witness while he is in The Hague. That is the primary reason why we sought to add them to the list, Your Honours, it was a review of the documents relate that he could legitimately comment on that caused us to believe that it would benefit the Court if the witness, while here in The Hague, exercised his opportunity to do so. And those are my submissions, Your Honour. I would respectfully ask that he just be allowed to comment the issue as to whether or not they be received in evidence, be reserved, and he will be in The Hague for a few days. Your Honours, the issue of prejudice probably will be remedied in those days while he is here, and we could undertake to let him remain for a little longer, if there are problems. May it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, before you sit, do I understand correctly that in most cases these 17 documents were tendered in evidence in the Milutinovic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In all cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All of these 17 documents, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were they tendered in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, not all of them. I am not sure if any of them were. I do believe that -- I know that not all of them were but I'm not sure if any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the Milutinovic case were they tendered by the Prosecution or the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Most of them were tendered by the Prosecution. I can see by the numbers, but I am not sure of some of them, of the last -- the last six. I could probably get verification of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So they were Prosecution documents for the purposes of the Milutinovic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I believe the last six were. I'm just looking at the numbers and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The numbers may not provide an answer. It depends whether a document was merely put to a witness by the Defence but not tendered, and it might then be tendered in re-examination, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, indeed, Your Honours. So -- I -- the numbers indicate to me that the majority were tendered and brought by the Defence; however, those that might be from the numbers, Prosecution documents, they might also have been brought by the Defence. I could not be sure about that here and now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If they were Prosecution documents, the question of how an omission of this nature could occur becomes more pressing. Are you able to assist us in any particular about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I do know that in reviews of the documents from the Milosevic [sic] case an effort was made - and there was a short period of time, but I'm not complaining about the time we had between that one case to move on to this case - an effort was made to winnow out of the material in the MOS case which was huge. Some of the material that we thought might not be of -- of great importance to the issues, the separate issues in this case; and it is probable that in that exercise which was done very quickly between the end of the MOS case and when we had to file the 65 ters that these might have been removed. These are all military documents and that is a -- I think that is the probable reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When you say "MOS" case you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- Milutinovic and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Milutinovic. I'm so sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic also mentioned being served at the same time or about the same time with a total of over 1.000 pages of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am trying to make inquiries into that, Your Honours. I do know that when we receive what are called -- when we receive searchs of the system of documents that relate to the witness, any material that the witness has testified before is disclosed immediately or as soon as possible to the Defence. What I believe is the situation in this case is that his testimony in the Milosevic case, his testimony in the Milutinovic case, and all of his testimony related to the matters that are before this Court was disclosed to Defence a long time ago, from early in the case and probably again when the 65 ters were filed. I am not sure what material the counsel for the Defence is speaking of, but there might have been documents that came up on recent searches that related to evidence that he might have given in other cases or in Belgrade in other matters that came -- that we have received in our evidence archives that came -- that have come up in searches and have been disclosed to the Defence. These would be disclosed as soon as the searches reveal that we have them, but if -- I could only give precise answers if I'm told what precisely those documents were that he speaks of, but the practice is to disclose this material as soon as they come up in the electronic searches of the archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, even in this case you seem to have had two bites at the cherry; the original motion, and then on Sunday evening another group of documents. Is there a simple reason why that should have occurred?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That -- without going too much into administrative issues, that was just a miscommunication on my part. I probably should say as to what documents should be included, what documents we would want to show him -- show the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have more, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence is open for cooperation. I think Mr. Stamp put a proposal acceptable to us, and I believe it will contribute to a more efficient proceedings. There will be a need that we be given some time, given that this will obviously last a few days at least. I see that the Prosecutor put five hours for this live testimony, and that will probably increase, during which time we'll be able to study those documents. I've just received information that we haven't even identified some eight documents that we received. We would need precise reference, and we will do our utmost to process these documents; however, we stand by that part of our objection requesting that the Bench should see to it that some documents be not introduced through this witness that we believe should not be introduced through him. This refers to his expertise. And it's a different issue whether such documents could be admitted through this witness if he were used as an expert witness or if this is merely a signature recognition witness, as I have just explained, who says, Well, I simply passed by this or that building, and I know where that was. In any case, we will make an effort, along the proposal of Mr. Stamp, to do this. Perhaps we may require a little bit more time to prepare, provided all these documents can be admitted through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are thankful for the submissions of counsel. The Chamber takes the view at the moment that this very unfortunate chapter may be able to be dealt with without undue difficulty and without, certainly, undue prejudice to the Defence if as each of these 17 documents are reached in the course of evidence of the witness, the issue of whether the witness is able to speak of personal knowledge or not is raised and able to be dealt with. So that if there's a document which is beyond the scope of what is properly the evidence of that person as a lay witness, that matter can be dealt with that way. Clearly we will need to deal with each document separately to reach a decision on that subject. With respect to the bulk of the submission, the question of whether or not the documents can be admitted in evidence will depend upon the degree of prejudice and whether it can be overcome with some moderate delay to enable the Defence to give consideration to the document. We say that accepting, as counsel has, the clear likelihood of relevance and of reliability of these documents. And we there focus our attention on the question of prejudice, and we do that against the background that no real justification is offered which would enable us to adjust the scales in favour of the Prosecution. So we must look at this from the eyes of the Defence and look at the question of prejudice accordingly. But it does seem to us that it could well prove to be the case that if documents are considered and marked for identification, it will be possible in the course of the week for Mr. Djurdjic to be in a position to cross-examine in respect of those documents, even if it does mean that we move to the next witness, deal with the next witness, and then come back to finish the evidence of this witness, that could well give additional time. We will see. So the position becomes this, Mr. Stamp, and I'm sure you will be thankful for Mr. Djurdjic, for his cooperative attitude, that you can proceed and present these documents to the witness. They will not be admitted into evidence at this stage, though. If they are used, they will be marked for identification. And we will then, if necessary, delay the cross-examination on those documents, perhaps by having another witness called and dealt with before coming back to this, and we will see whether by that process the prejudice that clearly is presently obtaining can be overcome to enable the matter to be dealt with and the evidence to be admitted. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We are ready then for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Stamp has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General Vasiljevic. Can we start by you telling us your full name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Aleksandar Vasiljevic, I was born on the 8th of July, 1938. Place of birth Vitkovic, municipality of Kraljevo, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I understand that you had a long career in the military. Can you give us an outline, a brief outline, of your career in the military of Yugoslavia, the former Yugoslavia and Serbia from start to finish.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: After secondary school, I graduated from the military academy in 1961. For three years I occupied command posts in units. In 1964 I was admitted into security organs of the Yugoslav People's Army; after that, I graduated from a one-year security school. And throughout all the time until 1988, I occupied security positions from basic positions within a battalion to the highest-level duties in the army and in the Federal Secretariat for People's Defence. In the meantime, I graduated from command staff academy in 1973, and I graduated also the war college, as it was called then, or the National Defence School in 1977. And in 1986, I was seconded from the Sarajevo army into the security administration in Belgrade as head of the counter-intelligence department. After that, since I had met the conditions for promotion into the rank of general, the criteria being that I had to leave the security apparatus and occupy some other posts outside the security service, so within -- between 1988 to 1990 I was a division -- motorised division commander in Sarajevo, where I received my rank of general. After that, I was transferred back to the security administration. I was assistant head or deputy head of the security administration in 1991. In June, I became head of the security administration of the JNA. I held that post until the 8th of May, 1992, when I was pensioned off among a large number of generals; 70 generals were pensioned off in that wave, halving practically the body of generals of the former JNA. I was retired until the 27th of April, 1999, when I was re-activated under the war conditions prevailing in Yugoslavia at the time. I was appointed deputy head of the security service of the VJ. One year later, I was appointed security advisor to the Chief of the General Staff, and I was pensioned off again towards the end of 2000 -- and on the 31st of March, 2001, officially my duties ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were pensioned off in 1992, what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I was major-general at the time, and in 1999 I was promoted to lieutenant-colonel-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you ended your service in the VJ in 2001, what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I was lieutenant-general at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in the course of your career in the JNA and later on when it became the VJ, did you receive awards and decorations for your work?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is a number of decorations. First of all, I have to explain that there was a practice whereby if you are successful in your post on average every five years one can receive a medal or a decoration. Out of those decorations that I received, there is one which is not your run-of-the-mill decoration. In 1990, I was decorated with a decoration for courage. I was also decorated after the end of the war in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that you spent your career in the security administration of the JNA and later on the VJ -- I should rephrase that: that you spent most of your career in the security administration of the JNA and later on the VJ. Could you explain to us what is the security administration or what was it at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be more precise, it would be more correct to state that most of my military career I spent in security organs of the JNA at different positions within units starting from battalions up to an army and the Federal Secretariat for People's Defence. Security administration is the umbrella and top organisation which controls and commands security organs in subordinated units. I spent four years there, two terms of duty, from 1986 to 1988, and from 1990 to 1992. Should I explain the remit and the tasks of organs of security within the JNA? I can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That indeed was my next question. What was the role and function of the security organs in the JNA and the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That is a two-fold service: Counter-intelligence, first, and prevention, functions of the security organs. The counter-intelligence activities are directed at detecting, monitoring, surveying, and prevention. Intelligence activities, through agents, earlier extreme émigrés that used to work against the armed forces and Yugoslavia in general, and also persons working illegally and in an organised manner to destroy the constitutional order of the country. The constitutional order was defined through criminal offences in chapter 20 of the penal code. There is a catalogue of criminal offences of such nature from stealth of weapons, disrupting defence capabilities, organising illegal enemy groups, sabotages, et cetera. This was part of the counter-intelligence effort which was the basic activity of the security organs. 90 per cent of working tasks in security organs were focused on counter-intelligence, and this is the raison d'etre of such security organs. The other string of duties was preventive, which means supporting command organs to organise preventive security measures, such as, setting up a protection system for military installations, taking actions to prevent theft of documents or weaponry, to organise security measures in combat operations, general measures that are applied anywhere. There is, I believe, a sixth or seventh item which details security measures for documents or weaponry of a security officer within a command is in charge of detailing out such security measures pursuant to the commander's order and to see to it that those measures are implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In seeking to achieve the tasks and assignments of the security organs, what would their sources of information be?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Counter-intelligence effort and collection of information on issues of subjects came from different sources. One of the major sources was a live person living in a community or, in a context, in a position where it has been assessed that there was some enemy activity or that there is intelligence that actual enemy activities were going on. We called such people collaborants of the security organs in our parlance, and the relationship with such sources was defined by law. There were of course mutual obligations in such a relationship. The second source of such intelligence could relate to specific, technical, or other methods applied by security organs, and -- which are subject to special approvals pursuant to law. In the JNA, the lowest-ranking officer who could approve such measures or methods was army commander. So security officers, even the head of the security administration, did not have the right to order secret surveillance, wire-tapping, or methods which violate certain rights and entitlements, but the constitution said that under certain circumstances such measures could be applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there a system in place - and I'm speaking primarily in 1999 but also generally - for the security organs to report up to security administration, where you were assigned, the information that they received through their operations?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: All security organs at all levels are duty-bound, when coming upon information and intelligence from within their purview, to report back on such -- along two lines: The first basic reporting line was to relay such intelligence to the immediate superior security officer. So if we're talking about a brigade security officer who may collect some intelligence or security service data, he would report to the corps security officer who would then assess the importance of such intelligence. If he can deal with it at his level, then there is no obligation to forward such intelligence upwards towards the army command. Then selection is done at army level command and security administration would receive -- select information of such importance that merit that these be imparted to the Chief of the General Staff and the head of the security administration, that this would be the vertical reporting. But there is also horizontal reporting. If there is some piece of information which is not of counter-intelligence interest - and I explained and described counter-intelligence activities - but is of importance for the overall security of the unit, then whoever comes upon it is duty-bound to inform of such information to the superior officer because security organs in the JNA were subordinated to their unit commanders in terms of discipline and others. In terms of subordination towards the superior security officer, there they were subordinated only within their purview. And the lowest level where counter-intelligence information could be imparted to a commanding officer was the army commander. All other information of general importance for military units were regularly given to commanders usually at collegium meetings that commanders convened, but also whoever had this information could seek a personal meeting with the commander to impart it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you were reinstated on the 25th of April, 1999, into the VJ. May I just backtrack a little. In your last answer you referred a couple times to the JNA. Your answer, I take it, also applies to the situation that obtained within the VJ, as it later became; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the system was more or less the same. There was one change, though. Earlier, the approval for the application of special measures for counter-intelligence activities or the so-called technical measures or tactical measures applied by security organs used to be approved at the lowest level by the -- an army commander. After the JNA ceased to exist and when VJ took over, the threshold of reporting on counter-intelligence matter was elevated to the level of Chief of the General Staff. This was the only difference, but the obligations in terms of reporting horizontally and vertically remained the same, horizontally to the unit commander and vertically to the superior security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I take it that you are saying that the change is that after the JNA ceased to exist, the so-called technical measures and tactical measures could only be approved by the Chief of the General Staff in the VJ? Is that what you meant by your last answer?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. You said that you were reinstated in April, the 27th of April, 1999. Can you briefly tell us the circumstances in which you were reinstated to the security administration of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I was pensioned off on the 8th of May, 1999 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1992. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in some special circumstances. Those special circumstances were as follows. Out of the 70 generals, only two generals did not meet a single requirement for pension. The conditions were either being at least 57 years old or having 40 years of work experience. I and my deputy were the only two not to meet either of these requirements. We were pensioned off due to the general situation, and it would take too much time for me to explain it all now. We were basically removed from the army. In 1999, when the aggression on Yugoslavia began, quite a number of the officers that had been pensioned off previously, both generals and lower-ranking officers, put themselves at the disposal of the General Staff of the army, should there be any need for their assistance irrespective of their former rank. Together with a group of security officers, I put myself at the disposal of the armed forces. On the 28th, I believe, of March an interviewer conversation took place between myself and General Geza Farkas, who was head of security. He mentioned that there was a possibility that I be assigned activities coordinator between the Military Security Service and the State Security Service of the Republic of Yugoslavia. I accepted that proposal; and after a whole month, I believe, around the 25th of April was when I was contacted for the first time after that. The Chief of General Staff, General Ojdanic, summoned me to his office, saying that in the security service they changed their mind about having a military officer around. Therefore, I was going to be appointed security advisor of the Chief of General Staff. Prior to that, Mr. Milosevic, the Yugoslav president, wanted to see me. On the 25th of April, I went to his office. If you're interested in what it was we discussed I can tell you but perhaps there is no need. He changed the decision and ordered that I become deputy head of the security service of the VJ rather than a security advisor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to move closer to the microphone and that all other microphones be switched off during the time he's answering. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mentioned that General Geza Farkas was head of security. Just tell us, he was head of which security?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: He was the head of the army security service of the VJ. The official title was head of security administration of the VJ. In terms of professional command, he was in charge of all security organs within the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you were appointed his deputy by President Milosevic, did General Farkas indicate to you what your tasks and assignments would be in the security administration?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: There was no need for him to explain to me what the role of a deputy head of security administration is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thanks. Did he appoint you to any particular area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Basically, my activities as the deputy head of security administration was to be in charge of all counter-intelligence activities of the security administration. In terms of establishment, the way the security system is set up, that function or that post is officially called deputy head of security administration who is also deputy --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- assistant for counter-intelligence. A person appointed to that position stands in for the head of administration in his absence. Therefore, there was no need -- if there was a need for a collegium meeting, the deputy would attend it. However, basically he was the deputy in charge of counter-intelligence. He was in charge of all professional activities of the security organs. When I was reinstated, President Milosevic divided that unified function between two people. I was appointed deputy, and Colonel Branko Gajic, who before the war was deputy and assistant for counter-intelligence, was appointed to the other part of the post which is assistant for counter-intelligence. This effectively meant that the two of us exercised the functions previously performed by one person. Both myself and Mr. Gajic dealt primarily with counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to just ask you to briefly describe to us the structure of the VJ during war time, during the NATO intervention, when a state of war was declared. Who was the overall commander of the VJ during the war?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The supreme commander, as far as I know, according to the constitution, did not exist as such. Previously when the JNA was in place, the supreme commander was a collective Presidency, the Presidency of the former SFRY, meaning to say that the eight members of the Presidency constituted the Supreme Command. The president of the Presidency - and that function was something that people rotated in - had the executive function in commanding the army pursuant to the Presidency decisions. In the latter period, during the VJ and the FRY times, the armed forces were in charge basically of the Supreme Defence Council. And the person presiding over the council was also the president of the FRY. His was the executive function to convey orders to the armed forces pursuant to the Supreme Defence Council decisions. In addition to the president of the FRY, in the Supreme Defence Council there were also presidents of Serbia and Montenegro. Another standing function on board was the chief of the military cabinet who was in charge of all technical aspects. When the war broke out, the Montenegrin president, Momir -- his last name escapes me, I think Djukanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Djukanovic --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: -- he left the Presidency because of certain issues, and then what was in place was a Rump Supreme Defence Council, meaning to say that Mr. Milosevic was there alongside Mr. Milutinovic. However, there were other members who occasionally participated in peacetime in the work of the Supreme Defence Council. Usually it was the Chief of the General Staff, the minister of defence, and other people who may be summoned depending on the agenda to be discussed --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: -- it was President Milosevic who was in charge of that function that one may call supreme commander. The General Staff of the VJ, under such circumstances as well as during the time of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, took on the role of the staff of the Supreme Command. Perhaps this is a broader answer to your question, but I foresaw perhaps a future question of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but for the time being can we just focus on the situation as it was during the period after the 24th of March, 1999, when a state of war was declared. You said the president then, Milosevic, would be the supreme commander and he would have a staff. Who were the members of the staff that the president as supreme commander had?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the meantime, while the translation is going on, can I ask that we bring up 06 -- sorry, 02601.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, could you just describe the staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Command Staff was headed by the Chief of the General Staff, General Ojdanic. I will have to use my glasses, given my eyesight and the number of years that have passed. His deputy was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, is this a witness's schematic or who drew it up since the witness is supposed to comment on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can do it without it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't matter. I just want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a schematic that the witness can identify and speak to. The purpose of this schematic is to set out in graphic form what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it a schematic prepared by the Prosecution or is it an official document --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's a schematic prepared by the Prosecution to show the witness's evidence in a graphic way to represent the evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The evidence is clear. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look at this document does this document indicate to you that the military forces that -- and the chain of command in respect to the military forces that were relevant in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, this is not a schematic of the Supreme Command Staff. This could be a schematic representing the organisation of the VJ. Why do I say this? because the Supreme Command Staff comprises the Chief of the General Staff with his assistants and heads of aspects and branches and services. I wanted to have my glasses on because it -- this would entail referring to a number of people, but this would be a rough chart of the way the VJ was organised. At the Supreme Command Staff, its head was the Chief of the General Staff, General Ojdanic. His deputy was General Marjanovic. Assistants to the Chief of the General Staff for the air force was General Velickovic, who was killed during the war and replaced by another person; then assistant for the navy was Admiral Nonkovic. And I can go through each and every one of them, but there is at least a dozen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think maybe my last question wasn't clear. I was asking if this was a schematic that indicates the forces that were -- the VJ forces that were relevant to Kosovo in 1999 and the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia had its 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Army. The first one was the Belgrade Army. The 2nd Army was in Podgorica, in Montenegro. However, some of its forces were in Sandzak and in Serbia itself. The 3rd Army is the Nis Army, within whose area was the southern part of Serbia and Kosovo. The 3rd Army comprised two corps, the Nis Corps and the Pristina Corps. Some forces of the Nis Corps and some forces of the 2nd Army, of whose command was in Podgorica, were engaged in Kosovo during the war by virtue of resubordination. Some units which did not organically belong to the 3rd Army were used to strengthen it by using certain brigades or military territorial detachments. The 3rd Army had two basic operational strategic units, these being the Nis and Pristina Corps. Among the more important organs, it had two districts: The Nis and Pristina Military District. The corps comprised a number of brigades, independent battalions, service regiments, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the area of responsibility of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps for the most part encompassed the area of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And also you mentioned the Pristina Military District. What was their zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The Pristina Military District also encompassed the area of Kosovo and Metohija; and in terms of the geographical distribution, it had branches in various municipalities such as Prizren, Djakovica, Pec, Urosevac, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 3rd Army in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It was General Nebojsa Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's General Vladimir Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know brief -- and if you could be brief in your answer, whether or not the normal chain that you see here with the General Staff headed by Colonel Ojdanic being between the supreme commander was always respected by General Pavkovic? In other words, do you know if General Pavkovic normally or always respected the normal chain of command going up?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: To the extent I am familiar with the situation, for the most part he respected the chain of command. I can explain why I say "for the most part."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If you could be very brief, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Briefly then, in Pristina as of 1998, objectively speaking, there was an organ in place called the Joint Command. That body was supposed to encompass the activities of the VJ and MUP in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. Occasionally, certain activities that had to be ordered directly from the general -- Supreme Command Staff to the 3rd Command and were to be implemented pursuant to the further decisions of the Joint Command, and then in turn the staff was supposed to be informed of the decisions made by the Joint Command. I know of certain documents following which the Chief of General Staff warned the 3rd Army commander that those planned activities should not be implemented the way that was envisaged, but in some other way. However, he did not use the customary term which would be "I order you to do so," but rather, I warn you that this or that should be done in a different way. This was rather unusual in terms of military hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. We'll get to that and to the Joint Command. But basically do you know if General Pavkovic always reported up through the Supreme Command Staff or if he sometimes bypassed General Ojdanic and the Chief and the Supreme Command Staff and went straight to Mr. Milutinovic, the supreme commander -- Mr. Milosevic, I beg your pardon, the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: These are two separate issues. The first one, whether he reported regularly to the Supreme Command Staff, yes, he did by virtue of daily combat reports. All units starting with brigades and up to the Supreme Command Staff were expected to report daily. The daily reporting was always followed through. The other issue is whether the 3rd Army commander without the knowledge of his immediate superior, General Ojdanic, communicated with the supreme commander -- well, that happened as well. It happened, and I was in a situation to see that myself. He didn't notify his superior General Ojdanic of being in Belgrade and that he was to see the state president, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: State president being President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 02601, Your Honours, I would ask that it be received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00883, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you took up your responsibilities in the latter part of April, 1999, did you receive information from your subordinates and your sources about events in Kosovo that were relevant to security and criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I could give you a very extensive answer. If you have in mind when it was that I received information for the first time, then I can be precise about that, and I suppose this is what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I was reinstated on the 27th of April, and I went to office that day. On the 8th of May, a security officer from the organ of the Pristina Corps came to the security administration. It was the then-Lieutenant-Colonel Djurovic who was deputy of the chief of security for the Pristina Corps. He was there for another reason concerning the case of a paramilitary unit which was absorbed by the VJ. In addition to that problem that we tried to resolve, I inquired of him to tell me what was happening in the field. He told me then that there were individual cases of crimes, rape, murders, and that there were other paramilitary formations in the territory in addition to the Jugoslav Petrusic group that we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm going to ask you to continue with your answer, but I just want to just get something clear. When he was reporting to you, did he report to you as part of his duty and report to you in your official capacity, or was this informal?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: This was a subordinate/superior type of contact. It could not have been informal --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: He simply notified me of some events that they omitted to inform us along the regular lines of reporting. Because of what he told me then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, I don't think you finished telling us all that he told you. You were telling us that there were cases of crimes, of rape, murder, and other paramilitary formation in the territory in addition to Jugoslav Petrusic's group. Could you tell us about the paramilitary formations and also Jugoslav Petrusic's group?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The Jugoslav Petrusic group numbered 25 persons who did not respect the standard procedure they would have to undergo to be accepted by the centre for volunteers in Brocna near Belgrade. A colonel from the General Staff intervened instead issuing them with uniforms without registering them individually and sending them to another volunteer reception centre in Medja near Nis; and they were issued weapons there. They were then sent to the Pristina Corps and its 125th Brigade, from whence they were sent to the border at Kosare. In terms of information the security service had, Jugoslav Petrusic was an agent of the French DST security service. We were warned via President Milosevic that we had a French agent amongst our ranks. That's why the Pristina Corps assistant for security was contacted to verify that. In any case, a few days later they were withdrawn from the field, disarmed, and arrested by the security organs of the VJ. Those arrested were Jugoslav Petrusic and his deputy Mr. Orasanin. There was an investigation which lasted for a month which resulted in an epilogue. That was the one paramilitary group. As for the other paramilitary groups in the field for which there were indications that they had committed crimes, he specifically mentioned the Skorpion unit. They arrived in Kosovo as part of the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit commanded by Colonel Trajkovic. In his words, upon their arrival in Podujevo they went house to house killing, in his words, a dozen children and two women. The 12 persons were allegedly killed, and once he learned of that, they were immediately expelled from Kosovo. That was one event he described. Another event had to do with the information he had that in Kosovo Polje there were members of Arkan's guard. That was the initial information we had regarding those events, and I put that down in my notebook, after which I ordered to him that they should send a written report to the security administration on that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On that note, Your Honours, I'm wondering if it might be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 4.15, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before I forget, General, you said that you had some knowledge of General Pavkovic bypassing General Ojdanic. Can you just tell us when in terms of the approximate month and year, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Mid-June 1999. I had a contact with a person, but he testified in private session, it's irrelevant who that person was, but I can name him. I sought from the head of security administration and the Chief of General Staff the green light to meet that person, and after the meeting with that person I reported back to General Ojdanic. But the state security division had reported that I had this contact with the opposition member and General Ojdanic was summoned to discuss this matter. General Ojdanic and I had arrived earlier to this meeting with Milosevic, and when we were 100 metres from the White Palace, General Pavkovic emerged from the White Palace and went in the direction of his car. General Ojdanic told me, Can you see him? He's coming to Belgrade without prior notifying me at all. When we attended this meeting with President Milosevic, General Ojdanic reacted and brought this matter to the president, and he said, President, please do not have my subordinates coming to your residence without prior clearance from me. And President Milosevic said, No, well, he was on a private matter, unofficially. And General Ojdanic told me that General Pavkovic was more frequently reporting immediately to Mr. Sainovic, who was in the Joint Command in Pristina, than him as Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could return now to the information that was reported to you by the security officer from the Pristina Corps in Kosovo. The crimes that we were talking about, the serious crimes, the rapes, the looting, the murders; did he say who committed them or the members or the organisations that the persons who committed them were from?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you mean the first meeting with Lieutenant-Colonel Djurovic or my tour of Kosovo from the 1st to the 7th of June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: First meeting.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: What emerged there were the first information about the scope that I already mentioned. After the first information about the so-called Skorpion group, which is not a usual term for unit in the military and in MUP because they have their own establishment titles, and after learning that Djurovic had learned that they came from Vojvodina, those persons, I ordered our counter-intelligence group in Novi Sad who was working out on the ground to check who those persons were and report back everything that they had learned about them. And four days later, in May, I received a report that it went for 120- to 150-strong group depending on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. Maybe you should slow down. This now is very, very important so -- and I'm not sure of the interpretation -- if you are going too fast for the interpretation. You remember the date you received the report from your organs from Novi Sad, the date in May, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of May I received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the report -- what did the report say was the result of your investigations of this Skorpion group?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to slow down. What was stated in the report was that the group was headed by Slobodan Medic, also known as Aca [as interpreted], and that the group he organised around himself comprised of 120 to 150 people, that there were practically two groups who went to Kosovo, one that was organised by Slobodan Medic, a.k.a. Boca, at the initiative of Mrgud Milanovic who in 1991 had been appointed there in Slavonia as minister of defence and that the other group was organised and led by Dalibor Novakovic. The report also said that in essence those persons had experience in battle-fields in former Yugoslavia, that among them were persons who had criminal records but no names were named there, and that they had returned from Kosovo a couple of days earlier. And since the check was conducted between the 8th and the 12th of May, we could say that they had returned from Kosovo at the beginning of May and that they were preparing another group to depart for Kosovo and that that group was being organised by Sokolovacki Zivan but his nickname was Zivan Chetnik. So this was the initial intelligence that we received identifying this person Medic, a.k.a. Boca, as the organiser of that group. They had been engaged as security detail around oil wells in Slavonia after they had ceased their operations in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Briefly, in maybe a sentence or two, did your operative report indicate what their reputation was in respect to what they had been up to on the battle-fields in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know specifically what [Realtime transcript read in error "that"] they had done there. I know they appeared as an organised group in the so-called Bihac operation. Similarly, there were some MUP units, JSO to be more precise, in that area. The general classification was that there were criminal types in their ranks, problematic people, which was written in the dossiers of those people who had returned from battle-field.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You had mentioned earlier that they went down there as part of the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit commanded by Zivko Trajkovic. Which organisation was that anti-terrorist unit a part of?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: SAJ as a special unit belonged to the public security division of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned that they -- your security organ from Pristina told you about Arkan's guards. Did he tell you what they were engaged in Kosovo and whether or not they were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic -- just a moment, please, if you would, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an intervention, page 35, line 7 of the transcript. It should read I do not know specifically what they did or what they had done. What is required is the word "what" and not the word "that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was asking you about the information on that first occasion you received in respect to the conduct of Arkan's guards and whether they were associated with any organisation or formation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: What we received was general information when Djurovic said that all those things had been going on in Kosovo and that there were also paramilitary formations outside the classical organisation of the military and the MUP. He mentioned that in Kosovo Polje they registered the presence of Arkan's guards there who were not part of any legal structures per establishment. But there was no details about what was the number of them there. We learned that subsequently. Information was that there was a camp at Kosovo Polje housing them. On the 8th of May there was no broader information about that, but of course on other occasions we received information on that, and I can discuss those subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we will, but I want to take it step by step. Just briefly, what type of reputation did Arkan's guards have in security circles, if I may put it that way?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I could tell you what their reputation was in military security circles; I cannot tell you about the overall security circles or community. Arkan's armed units had been registered as early as the beginning of 1991, at the time when I worked in the security administration. We received operative reports about that initial group containing -- comprising of 21 persons. We did some security checks on who those persons were, what was the structure of the group; and out of the 21 members, they had collected convictions of 105 years of prison sentences on average five years of prison sentence each, which means that they had come from criminal background. Later on, that unit was expanded. If I were to go back to the Vukovar and January 1992 when they were supposed to be disbanded and expelled from the area of Srem and both eastern and western Srem, at that time the order on their expulsion from the Vukovar area was transmitted or relayed as an order by General Zivota Panic and it was relayed by Colonel Petkovic. What I mean to say, there were 150 of them at that point in time and that a person from the state security division of MUP of Serbia, Badza Stojkovic, said that there would be no problem regarding that that they would enter a special unit formation of theirs. Their reputation was of crime, of different types of crime that they had committed. But let me cut a long story short. May we -- may I add that they wore rifles in Belgrade, in central Belgrade, as security detail of the premises of the SSJ party and nobody objected. At Arkan's funeral they also wore automatic rifles and nobody objected to that. Most of them had MUP personal cards or identity passes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's stick to 1999. When you say "most of them had MUP personal cards," did the personal cards relate to the state security section of the MUP or the public security section of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not clear as to the interpretation of the security detachment and security division. No, they were more in line with the state security division of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I can take it then that these ID cards were issued by the state security sector or division?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I presume so. I cannot tell you specifically because I never saw them. I know about the -- Arkan's official pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were also told that there was a second group from the Vojvodina area or the Novi Sad area that was sent to Kosovo, that is the group of Dalibor Novakovic. Can you comment on that? Did you receive information on that first occasion whether or not this group was in fact sent to Kosovo and were they integrated into any formation there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Initial information referred only to the Slobodan Medic group and that that group had returned at the end of April/beginning of May but also was informed that Dalibor Novakovic's group was being prepared to leave. And then there was a third group of Zivan Chetnik, these were the persons who organised these groups. One such group was organised by Goran Hadzic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were these groups -- did you ultimately learn whether these groups were dispatched to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I cannot state with any degree of reliability.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, the information you received from - I'm probably going to get the name wrong - from Mr. Djurdjicic [sic] or from your Pristina Corps operative should -- and I'm not referring to counsel, should that have been reported up through the chain of command to the General Staff where you were or to the security administration?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that should have been written down as information of the Pristina Corps security organ, and it should have been sent to the security department of the 3rd Army. And then the security department of the 3rd Army would decide whether to report on that briefly to the security administration, but they did not forward this information, neither to the Nis army security department - because I later on verified that - and on that occasion I ordered Djurovic, when he relayed that oral information, to prepare a written note and to corroborate it with other details that we had no occasion to discuss at the time because he was in Belgrade on another matter. And that note was subsequently drafted. But out of the information that we received then, which included apart from the Jugoslav Petrusic group there were information -- there was information about soldiers raping some young girls in Kosovo, and I received names; and information that they had allegedly been prosecuted. I wanted him to write it down and announce that we would be coming to Kosovo to consider those matters. If you allow me, what was the outcome of all this? We received initial information, more complete information, from the counter-intelligence group of Novi Sad on the 12th of May. On the 13th of May, which was Security Services Day, on that occasion of that holiday, General Ojdanic, Chief of the General Staff, received a delegation of security circles. General Geza attended as well as I did and Colonel Branko Gajic. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's General Geza Farkas?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The then-Colonel Branko Gajic, who was promoted to general on the 16th of June, and I were there. General Krga, Branko Krga, head of the intelligence department administration of the General Staff. General Farkas informed General Ojdanic about -- what had been learned about the goings-on in Kosovo. This was the initial information to him. He was surprised, and he reacted promptly in front of our eyes. He phoned President Milosevic and literally said, Mr. President, I learned that all things -- all sorts of things are going on down there in Kosovo, that there are paramilitary groups, that there are rapings, murder. I don't know what Milosevic replied. After that conversation ended, Ojdanic told us, The President orders you to prepare all sorts of reports on such developments and to attend a meeting at the command post on the 17th of May, bringing those written reports. After that, General Ojdanic called General Pavkovic and asked him, Commander, what is going on down there? I don't know what the reply was. And then General Ojdanic said, On the 16th of May report back to me with all relevant information at a meeting here at the General Staff. And on the 17th of May there will be a meeting at President Milosevic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did that meeting of the 16th of May take place?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was attended again by General Geza, Colonel Branko Gajic, and I. By that time we had acquired more information because Djurovic from the Pristina Corps had sent a dispatch containing more details, particularly the presence of Arkan's units and that camp of theirs than individual details of crimes perpetrated individually by military personnel. I recall a Captain Stekovic, if I'm not mistaken, who murdered a number of Albanians. We had received more information supplementing the initial information we had received from the Pristina Corps, and General Pavkovic also came up with his information. On behalf of the security administration, I briefed them on what we had learned. Then General Pavkovic briefed us exhaustively about the developments in Kosovo, about the crimes committed by both members of the army and the MUP. When I spoke about the presence and the crimes in Podujevo and when I mentioned Slobodan Medic, General Pavkovic said that he had personally seen at Prolom Banja, Medic, with whom he had a brief contact. Medic was wearing a NATO-style uniform and wore SAJ insignia, the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit of Serbia. And that later on he had learnt from a general, I think General Djakovic, who had a lengthier discussion with Boca, and who had related to him that they had arrived to Kosovo following the orders of General Djordjevic of the MUP and that the MUP would collect them and send them to those areas where the situation was the worst out on the ground. And then General Pavkovic said he had notified Vice-President Sainovic of those things but he offered no special reaction to that. So they did have information that they had been expelled from the ground and that that had been done by the deputy commander of the SAJ Dragan Stojanovic or somebody else - and there was a nickname, but I forgot that man's family name - saying that that officer had expelled them from there. Furthermore, General Pavkovic referred that on the occasion of the murders and the corpses they had found on the ground, he said that they had suggested to General Lukic that they set up a Joint Commission to determine who might have been responsible for those crimes judging by the areas where those corpses were found, maybe the army or the MUP of Serbia or some third party --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Firstly, General Lukic was the chief of the MUP staff for Kosovo at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we go into what he said about a Joint Commission, did he say how many corpses they had found or were on the ground in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Later on in General Ojdanic's briefing, he complained of a degree of obstruction on the part of the MUP organs in Kosovo to try and deal with those problems. He stated that they were only sent a letter by the MUP to the Pristina Corps in which they said that there were around 800 corpses for which the VJ was responsible in terms of committing crimes. However, Lukic did not accept the proposal to establish a Joint Commission. Then General Pavkovic set up his own commission, and it was established that there were 271 corpses in the areas where the army was. There were 326 corpses in the area where MUP units were active. This gives us a total of 597 persons. That was the data provided by General Pavkovic based on the results of the work of his commission. Some people were inquiring about what kind of corpses those were. We all arrived at the same conclusion. These corpses were not victims of crimes. These people were killed in operations, either by NATO forces or VJ forces. But all of those corpses were not victims of crimes, but they were killed as a consequence of operations. General Pavkovic informed Mr. Sainovic accordingly, but we did not receive any particular feedback.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Firstly, if you could just have a couple brief answers to clarify one or two things. Did General Pavkovic explain about the difference between the 800 bodies that were reported found and the 597 bodies that could be associated with territory that either the MUP or the VJ controlled?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The initial information that MUP had was that the 800 corpses -- that those deaths were caused by the army; however, the commission's finding was that there were 597. As I said, the breakdown was 271 corpses in the army area and 326 in the MUP area. There were no 800 corpses, but 597. Am I clear on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Did General Pavkovic mention whether or not these corpses or some of these corpses had been exhumed; and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: He did not discuss that. It was my impression that this did not involve any exhumations, but rather that these corpses had simply not been buried by that time. No sanitation and hygiene measures were undertaken. I suppose preceding that it was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- it can be my assumption perhaps that some of these corpses were registered or reported as having been found, and therefore one would conclude that they had been buried, but it is only my presumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you said we all arrived at the same conclusions, these corpses were not the victims of crimes, these people were killed in operations, either by NATO forces or VJ forces; could you elaborate on that a little bit further? Is that what General Pavkovic reported to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I can provide a factual basis for that. I was in Kosovo with General Gajic between the 1st and 7th of June. We visited 12 security organs in subordinate units. At the end, at a meeting in Pristina, we collated all the information the army had per crimes and victims --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, if I may have a moment. Let's just focus for the time being on the 16th of May meeting. We are going to get to your tour of Kosovo a little bit later on. I just want to know if this is what -- if General Pavkovic had told you about the causes of death of the people that were in the military areas at that 16th of May meeting.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Did you decide upon any procedure in respect to the meeting that you expected to have the next day with President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: General Ojdanic said that all the matters that we discussed without skipping or avoiding anything should be passed on to President Milosevic. The decision was made to the effect that I was to put the army case to him; however, I declined, given that General Pavkovic had much more information than I did. I only had some initial information provided by my security organs. I briefed the meeting on the information we received through security organs, and General Pavkovic spoke about the information he had gathered along his chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You just said you briefed the meeting on information received through your security organs. Is that the meeting with the late President Milosevic you are speaking of now?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It was the meeting on the 17th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The meeting took place at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was present?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: From the army there was General Ojdanic, General Pavkovic, General Geza Farkas, myself, and Colonel Gajic; the five of us from the General Staff. The other attendees were President Milosevic, Vice-President Sainovic, and head of the state security sector Rade Markovic. There was no one there of the generals or people from the public security sector. Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic, minister of the interior, was not present either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did -- did the absence of the minister of interior or any of the generals from the public security sector strike you as -- well, I withdraw that. Let me ask you an open question. Did you form any conclusions as to the reasons for the absence of the head of the public security sector or the minister in a meeting of this nature?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't pay much heed. It was a bit odd that no one was present on that side, especially --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: -- if you had General Pavkovic, commander of the 3rd Army there, who was in the field in Kosovo. It would have been natural to have there at least General Lukic who, in a way, corresponded to him in rank. In any case, President Milosevic only briefly said that they were all busy and that they were in no position to attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall whether or not you made notes of what happened at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No. No notes were taken in terms of official minutes. People noted things down individually if they thought it was necessary. I usually have the habit of noting things down in meetings. Specifically concerning that meeting to the extent of what I could note down, I did keep notes as well as the then-Colonel Branko Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
