utterances.text: In my notebook, if I may, I did not make notes on the contributions of General Pavkovic or on my contribution because we had typed reports, papers, to present at that meeting. Therefore, you cannot find any of my or Mr. Pavkovic's contributions in my notebook because I believe those contributions should be in written form, typed somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up 65 ter number 02592.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Page 46, line 20, a part of the witness's answer is missing whereby the witness stated that those reports should be in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you identify the document there before you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I recognise it. It is a photocopy of a page in my notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is dated --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The 17th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is the record of your meeting that you just described?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At this meeting, did you give a report?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To the persons present at the meeting. Did you brief them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, not after the meeting. As I said, I intervened during the meeting as well as General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. So the question is: Did you brief them at the meeting as to what your security organs had discovered?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I think you also said Mr. -- or General Pavkovic also made a contribution.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have in your note here that General Pavkovic -- or that someone said - and tell us who said it - there is no problem with Petronijevic's group. Who said that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: It was Pavkovic's comment. Yes, it's a mistake, actually, it should be Petrusic, Jugoslav Petrusic's group, because by that time he had been arrested as well as Mr. Orasanin; that group had been disbanded, disarmed, and withdrawn from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the report that you gave and the report that General Pavkovic gave generally repeated the same matters that you had discussed the previous day, the 16th of May?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, after you gave these reports I have it here that Rade spoke. Who is Rade?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Rade was the head of the state security sector, Rade Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He said that the volunteers are a necessary evil. What did he mean by that? What did you understand him to mean.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it would be better if I describe that part of the meeting in order to give you a full context --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: -- but I can answer your individual questions as well. In any case, since I mentioned the presence of Arkan's Tigers in Kosovo Polje in my report, on that topic he said that it was correct that Arkan had contacted him offering about a hundred of his men. He only accepted around 30, provided they wore uniforms. He also said that he had learned the day before, the 16th, that some people, some among them, killed a married couple in Kosovo and that an investigation had been ordered and proceedings initiated. I think he said that they would be returned. Because of the hundred that was offered and since Medic's group was mentioned, he said, They are a necessary evil and one cannot win the war with 100 people, 100 men. Since in my intervention I refer to Medic Slobodan's group, Rade Markovic said he spoke with General Djordjevic, who told him that they had been withdrawn from Kosovo to Prolom Banja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you noted in respect to SM. Who is SM? Could you just tell us that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: SM is Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic said, Sit down with Vlajko and Rodja and clear it up with them. Their heads won't be chopped off, but Boca must answer. Who is Vlajko is who is Rodja?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: This intervention by President Milosevic represents his comment on what Rade Markovic had said in terms that he had spoken with General Djordjevic about Boca Medic and that he informed them that they had been withdrawn from Kosovo. He was actually turning to Rade Markovic and telling him, Convey to Vlajko and Rodja, Vlajko was the MUP minister, Vlajko Stojiljkovic; and Rodja is General Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And later on you have a comment here from Sainovic. Do you know what Sainovic's role was or could you just tell us now what Sainovic's role was in relation to the forces, the MUP forces and VJ forces, that were operational in Kosovo? And if you could tell us briefly, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I know that he spent some time in Kosovo. On the 1st of June, I attended a meeting of what was called the Joint Command. He was probably called to that meeting because he was responsible for overall activities down in Kosovo. That was his role. He offered a short comment saying that, Obviously with the SAJ they have certain habits on how to gather reserves or reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And Mr. Milosevic said, I support the work of the RDB and the security organs to have all cases of big Serbs resolved. What did you mean -- what is the meaning of this note?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The meaning has to do with the way the reserve forces of the MUP were being assembled. There were many of them representing themselves as big Serbs who, in his words, caused damage and that they tarnish the positive image of what was achieved in Kosovo. He meant it that way. He was referring to the way the MUP reserve force was being gathered, cherry-picking people such as Boca, Arkan's men, et cetera. I think he insisted greatly on the importance of dealing with Vlajko and Rodja in the sense that they have no reason whatsoever to protect such people. And having in mind Rodja and Vlajko, he said, Their heads would not fly because of that, their heads would not roll. That was the sense of his comment. He also wanted to sort of calm tensions down in terms of the reserve forces. There was mention made of people paying 500 or 1.000 German marks to get a uniform to be able to go to Kosovo in order to loot freely, but he said that at the time he had no knowledge of any presence of Arkan's men in Kosovo Polje or any camps of theirs. I can describe further the course of the meeting if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but may I just check something before you -- President Milosevic also said neither Vlajko nor Obrad nor Rodja have reason to protect them. Who is Obrad?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: MUP General Obrad Stevanovic who I encountered during my trip to Kosovo at the meeting of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was his function in the MUP, do you know?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: What I know is in terms of rank. He was the third-ranking man in MUP there. I think his function was assistant minister of internal affairs for special units of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who were the two people senior to him ?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot specify whether he was subordinated to assistant minister of internal affairs for the public security sector, General Djordjevic, or there were parallel assistants to the minister of the interior. I'm not familiar specifically with the chain of command. But from communications we all knew that they were heads of the public security sector of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. And the third person mentioned in this note, the translation has it as Radja, who is that person that Mr. Milosevic is referring to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, Rada should read -- maybe it should spell out Rade, Rade Markovic. It could be my long hand which could be illegible -- no, no, no, this is Rodja -- no, neither Obrad nor Rodja. Obrad Stankovic [as interpreted] and Rodja is General Djordjevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Obrad Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Obrad Stevanovic and Rodja is General Djordjevic. So it's not Rada or Rade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. What at that time did you understand to be President Milosevic's role in respect to the MUP, his de facto role I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: You know what, President Milosevic was president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Hierarchically speaking, Ministry of Interior is an integral part of the Serbian government. At that time there was no federal Ministry of the Interior, practically it did not function because of the state of affairs in Montenegro. So the minister of the interior was supposed to be linked directly to the president of the government or the prime minister. But since President Milosevic was president of Yugoslavia and through the force of his authority, he had direct links with the minister of the interior. And within the Ministry of the Interior, there are two key divisions: Public security division and state security division. Rade Markovic headed the state security division, and practically he was supposed to be subordinated to Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic. But in practice, ever since 1998 when head of the state security division was Jovica Stanovic [as interpreted] after Stojiljkovic became minister of the interior who wanted briefs from the state security division's head, Jovica Stanovic [as interpreted] did not want to accept that. He reacted very sharply, and he addressed President Milosevic about that matter, seeking that he remain in direct contact with him although he was then president of Yugoslavia otherwise he would resign from his position as state security division head. I know this on the basis of my conversations with State Security Service who were top brass of that department. And from then on --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. I think you are coming to the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: From then on, the state security division practically was directly subordinated and managed and controlled and ordered by Slobodan Milosevic and Rade Markovic was there on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In this -- in your note you record President Milosevic as saying that Vlajko, the minister, and I think you said earlier that the minister of interior was supposed to be linked directly to the president of the government or the prime minister, by that you mean that the minister of interior was supposed to be linked to the president or prime minister of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that this was regulated by regulations, by laws. So you know -- should I go further --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he could more be linked to the president of Serbia in some circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: However, we have the president of Yugoslavia, Mr. Milosevic, at this meeting saying, Neither Vlajko's nor Rodja's heads would be chopped off. Later on, Neither Vlajko nor Obrad nor Rodja have reason to protect them. What was President Milosevic's relationship, influence, or authority de facto in respect to the MUP and the public security sector of the MUP in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I already stated that practically those persons were under the direct jurisdiction of the president of Yugoslavia, namely, President Milosevic, Slobodan Milosevic. As you can see, President of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic, did not attend. Nominally he would have been supposed to have a more direct link of the minister of interior than the president of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The remainder of your notes, and I'm afraid we will not have time to go through all of it, but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please bear in mind the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Maybe I'm going too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's the background noise, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have had an opportunity, I understand, to review the remainder of your notes. Are they accurate as to what you recall to have transpired in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not read this note. I have only the first page shown to me, but I have no reason to believe that other pages are false. I can verify them for your purposes if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you flip to the next page and then the next, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we should turn the page. Now it's okay. Yes, you don't have to zoom in. I can see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, there are your notes of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 02592 and ask that it be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, will be assigned P00884.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see later on in the meeting somebody that you refer to as Saja spoke. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That was Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in English could we go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he said - and this is at the bottom of the first page: "... and there's the task of working on clearing up the terrain." What at that time did you understand that expression, "clearing up of the terrain," to mean?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Clearing up of the terrain is the professional term which implies that after combat operations what has to be conducted are smaller-scale operations to neutralise or destroyed residual enemy groups or another term that may be used in military circles, the pockets of resistance. Clearing up of the terrain in such documents should not be taken to mean sanitation of the battle-field. These are two separate operations. Clearing up of the terrain is a common term shared by both the military and the MUP implying dealing with residual or remaining enemy groups or forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. About this meeting that you had on the 17th, when you noted what General -- sorry, President Milosevic said in respect to Vlajko, Obrad, and Rodja, did they -- did what Mr. Milosevic said indicate to you what role or authority these three persons had in respect to the MUP forces in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. It was -- what was discussed there was the situation in Kosovo, not other security issues in the territory of Serbia and Yugoslavia. He addresses Rade Markovic to relay this message to those persons who bear the highest responsibility for the use of MUP forces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. After this meeting, did you receive any tasks from General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I feel the duty to expound my answer a bit. During the meeting, both General Pavkovic and General Ojdanic and Mr. Sainovic also concurred. They raised the issue that a special state commission should be dispatched to Kosovo to look into what was going on there. However, Mr. Milosevic did not offer any comment, and he bypassed this issue all together. What he offered in return was that obviously there were bad relations between the Military Security Service and MUP organs, probably on the basis of an earlier information coming from General Pavkovic that he had not encountered General Lukic's understanding on the establishment of a Joint Commission. He issued a task -- well, the only task issued then was for the relations to be cleared and that poor relations between those two services may be tantamount to sabotage, and that for that reason General Ojdanic had to convene a joint meeting with MUP organs at which those misunderstandings had to be cleared. This was the task that he issued. After that meeting, immediately after it, General Ojdanic ordered me and General -- Colonel Branko Gajic in the light of what had been said in the meeting to go to Kosovo as soon as possible, to contact our subordinate security organs, and to collect information on everything that was going on there, but also to perform a classical inspection tour of security organs in the light of their counter-intelligence activities. This was the tasks -- task we were issued by General Ojdanic, the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Incidentally before we move on to the task, at the end of the meeting did you military officers leave the office and could you tell us if anybody remained?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we rose after the meeting was over, we discussed the summary for people to leave the meeting. Rade Markovic also stood up, head of the state security sector, but President Milosevic told him, Rade, you should stay behind. So he stayed behind together with Mr. Sainovic in President Milosevic's presence. We had an impression that a conversation is going to take place or to be continued which would not welcome our presence. And we commented so and we stated so after emerging from the conference room.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You said General Ojdanic issued a task or gave a task to convene a joint might with the MUP organs in order to clear misunderstandings. Was this meeting -- were efforts made to convene this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. General Geza was tasked with convening the meeting with Rade Markovic; but in spite of repeated efforts to get in contact with him, the latter was always absent or otherwise engaged. So until July, the beginning of July, that meeting did not take place and Chief of the General Staff, General Ojdanic, had to insist for that meeting to take place. That meeting took place on the 9th of July, 1999, at the premises of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And we will get to that meeting later on. You indicated that you were also tasked the conduct or control of -- or an inspection tour of the security organs in Kosovo and also to make inquiries as to what was happening down there. Did you go to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We departed immediately after that meeting, General Gajic and I; but in the meantime, a serious incident with the 7th Brigade from Krusevac had occurred. That brigade used to be in Kosovo. Almost half of the brigade's ranks left their positions with weapons and materiel and returned to Krusevac. Because of this major incident, the two of us were tasked together with the head of security of the 3rd Army, Colonel Antic, to identify the ringleaders of this mutiny and to secure through the organs of the authorities in Krusevac the return of the army personnel and the weapons and materiel back to Kosovo. And only after we've dealt with the Krusevac situation we could depart for Kosovo on the 1st of July. I reached Kosovo together with General Gajic and Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the date?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: The 1st of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: So together with Colonel Antic, head of security of the 3rd Army, we reached Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, on the 1st of June in Pristina, did you conduct any work there in respect to your tasks or the tasks that you had been assigned?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The evening of the 1st of June we were briefed on the situation by the head of the security service of the Pristina Corps, Colonel Momir Stojanovic. However, military regulations order us, and it's a matter of ethics, is that whenever somebody comes to a command post, the commander should be informed of that. Colonel Stojanovic phoned General Pavkovic, telling him that I had arrived to Pristina. He expressed a wish for us to meet. He invited Stojanovic and me to come over to the command of the Pristina Corps where we could find him. At the time he did not indicate that that evening's meeting was going to be a Joint Command meeting. He just invited us over. The two of us went to the Pristina Corps command, to that building, and after greetings General Pavkovic told me, Well, stay here. We will have a meeting of the Joint Command. Why don't you attend it and after that we will have dinner. Soon afterwards persons started arriving, persons who were supposed to attend the meeting. First of all I have to say that my impression was that it was something as an operations centre. There were maps on the walls, there were officers doing their tasks, and there was a separate conference table seating --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What kind of operations centre?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the command post of the Pristina Corps, and that this room was operations centre to communicate with subordinate units and maintain maps of the present situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you arrived there with Colonel Stojanovic, who was present in the room?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I already stated that there was a number of officers, some of whom I knew and some of whom I saw for the first time. But of the key personnel, General Pavkovic was there, General Lazarevic as well, and the two of them attended the meeting. So of the military personnel, on the one hand you had Pavkovic, Lazarevic, and I sitting next to him, and then Colonel Momir Stojanovic. At the other end of the table were MUP generals, General Djordjevic, General Stevanovic, and General Lukic. A couple of minutes later, after we'd gathered there, Vice-President Sainovic arrived with some person from Kosovo whose family name I will remember for sure. We sat down and the meeting was opened by a brief on the current state of play that day --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you stop a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I wonder if we could go into private session just for one moment, Your Honour, just to ask the name of someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Then we will need to have the break, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We were at the meeting of the 1st of June, the Joint Command meeting. When Mr. Sainovic and the other person arrived, how were they treated by the MUP and VJ generals gathered there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic was accompanied by Mr. Andjelkovic. We all rose. When Sainovic sat down, we sat down as well. Mr. Andjelkovic sat on the side with the MUP generals, whereas Pavkovic was facing him from the side where the army representatives were. General Djordjevic briefly said that a MUP general was missing, I can't tell you what his name is, because he was busy in the field. I was a bit taken by surprise by that meeting. I did not take down detailed notes of who was present and who was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The other person that attended or the person who attended with Mr. Sainovic, you said Mr. Andjelkovic, that's Zoran Andjelkovic; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was his position at that time in respect to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't really know precisely what his position was, whether he was president of the Kosovo Executive Council or something else. In any case, he was one of the top politicians in Kosovo. I don't know what the exact name or title of his position would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you know General Djordjevic personally before that day, the 1st of June?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I know -- I knew from the media who General Djordjevic was; however, this was the first time I met him. I think we met on one other occasion at the meeting in the General Staff on the 9th of July. In any case, I had seen him on television; therefore, it was easy for me to recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the meeting on the 1st of June was he introduced?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, there were no introductions made. I knew General Lukic from before that; I greeted him before the session, and spoke to him briefly. I did not speak to the other generals there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you summarise for us what happened and what was said and by whom after the meeting began, that is, after Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Andjelkovic arrived?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while you're proceeding to do that, could I ask the Registrar if we could bring up ERN -- not ERN, 65 ter number 02862. Could we move to page 2 in the B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What you see there is a cover of your work notebook?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the photocopy of a cover -- of the cover page of my work notebook. We can see on the screen now the note pertaining to the 1st of June, 1999. In it I noted down briefly what was discussed at the Joint Command meeting. Perhaps I can continue what I tried -- what I started explaining at the outset. I said I was taken by surprise by that meeting. It was my custom to take notes of the meetings I participated in. I marginally wrote things down as to who said what at the meeting, and I did not include a list of attendees. I was not keeping minutes. I was not even an official at that meeting. In any case, I did take some very brief notes. I don't need to refer to this page. I can tell you some things from my memory. The first was General Lukic, after whom we had General Lazarevic speak. Then there was a quick interjection by Deputy President Sainovic, then we had Lazarevic and Pavkovic. It was my opinion that it was a daily reporting session or meeting of the past 24 hours. No broad issues were discussed. They only discussed what took place the day before and what was being planned for the next day. From what I recall, General Lukic briefly spoke about having information that in the area of Trpeza and Drenica there was a larger group of Albanian terrorists and that because of that they were preparing an operation that was to clear that area and deal with that group. For that purpose, they envisaged some 300 policemen to be used. Then he said that in the course of the previous day there were some activities dealing with a larger group of terrorists in the area of Jablanica and that their front -- their first defence line was broken through, causing casualties on their side. I believe he mentioned some 15 terrorists being killed, whereas only one policeman was wounded. After that we had General Lazarevic speak who referred to the situation in his area of responsibility. He may have gone outside of that topic on occasion. What was interesting for me was that some equipment or cargo was parachuted during the night. It probably was some sort of assistance for the terrorists, and he also mentioned an illegal radio station being in operation. Then he discussed the situation along the border with Albania and the well-known problems of extensive operations and many losses in the area of Kosare. During the day, seven soldiers were killed there and some 300 different types of projectiles were fired including rockets. He said that it was twice as many as the average of the days before that, which was around 160 rockets if I recall correctly. He also said that the losses were great. I knew of that from the reports of my security organs I had received since there was an MP battalion there in which at least 50 soldiers and officers were either killed or wounded. Then we have General Pavkovic, who expressed his dissatisfaction with the fact that certain positions and areas were not held on to. He believed that they were easily abandoned, and he even said that measures should be taken against the people responsible for that. He also stated that they had information that in Albania and Macedonia there were groups, larger groups, assembling which could mean that the beginning of a land operation could be expected from those areas. He also said that they noticed some 2.000 people in Albania along the border and the front line were active in one particular area which was about 6 kilometres. He also said or reiterated that every foot of land or building should be held onto and that -- and that operations should be intensified so as to avoid any surprises in the future. Mr. Sainovic agreed that the issues of Jablanica and Trpeza have to be dealt with in the next three or four days. That's what I recall, and I took some brief notes of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Two things, your notes in respect to Mr. Sainovic's contribution is that Mr. Sainovic tasked them with action to be completed within three or four days. What did you mean when you wrote that he tasked them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: About what was discussed before that, that there seems to be an operation prepared in Jablanica, Trpeza, and the border --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. But --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: -- and that we should deal with these terrorist sabotage groups --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm just focusing on when you say he tasked them. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall any particular tasks assigned to anyone. He probably spoke to the effect that such tasks should be implemented and distributed among the units. I simply noted down the gist of what I believed important and what I can recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the B/C/S we don't see that part of the document and -- nor does the witness. We only see the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Could we -- yes. I think the witness said that he can speak --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness said he didn't need to look at the document at the commencement of his evidence about this, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Having -- can you now answer my questions, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just a minute, General. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not react until the moment you started discussing the translation in the English version. It was then that I reacted, asking that we see the B/C/S version to see what is written. That was my reaction to your statement, and I have no idea what the witness will say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once I read this, I realise that this may have been unclear to the translator. It says, Sainovic assigned the task or a task that the operation be completed within three or four days. He issued a task, i.e., that the operation should be completed in three or four days, and I believe I said that even before I looked into the notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Having regard to your record and your memory, can you tell us what was your understanding of Sainovic's -- of Mr. Sainovic's standing and relationship in respect to Generals Lukic, Lazarevic, and Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic was deputy president of the federal government or deputy prime minister. He was one of the closest associates of President Milosevic. His authority was beyond dispute. He came from the very top of politics. He enjoyed trust for that reason, and he was there as a person representing Slobodan Milosevic in Kosovo. We were there discussing things when he and his escort came in, Zoran Andjelkovic, and then we all stood up. You can see from that that he was the central figure. You can also see that by the position he was seated at the table. There were neither Andjelkovic nor Pavkovic next to him. They were on the sides. It was my conclusion that he was a person of authority. He also concluded that the operation be undertaken, setting a dead-line of three or four days. I don't know whether I'd call that a command function. No one reported to him as it usually would be when reporting to a military officer, but obviously he was the most important person. People listened to him. He listened to the daily debriefing and concluded the meeting. I apologise if I spoke too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You said he concluded the meeting, which was going to be the next question I was going to ask you, but you have said it. What do you mean when you say he concluded the meeting? What can we gather from that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, people can have various interpretations, but I believe I've stated my conclusion. I'm not sure I should go any deeper than that. I stated the facts, and I leave it up to anyone's conclusion. I stated that I believe he was the person of most authority there, respected by others, and that the meeting began with his arrival. It was also concluded once he said, We're done, let's go and eat. I didn't write that down, but more or less that's the way it ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And thank you because it reminds me of another thing I need to ask you about this document. You don't have General Djordjevic's name here. Is there any reason why, as he was present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I have explained at the beginning that I was no notekeeper. I wasn't even ready to attend. Among other things, I also believe I omitted General Stevanovic, Obrad Stevanovic, although he was present. As far as I recall, since it seems I need to go into further detail and I believe Defence will have some questions as well, I wanted to say this: When I contacted The Hague Tribunal's office in Belgrade, I reported there as a suspect for certain crimes in Croatia. As regards Kosovo and whatever happened in 1999, I wasn't prepared to speak about that. However, given that the discussion included Kosovo, the OTP probably found the meeting in Pristina on the 1st of June interesting. I believe I then mentioned that Lukic did not intervene at the meeting, rather, it was General Djordjevic. Perhaps I even repeated that in the Milosevic case. However, when I was being proofed for the Milutinovic et al. case and referring to Kosovo, I started going through my notebooks and then I found Lukic as having contributed. Then when I said that he participated in the meeting and his Defence tried to deny that, I asked -- I consulted my notebooks. It was then that the Tribunal asked for the notes to be photocopied, showing that Lukic was in attendance. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: There is no dilemma that what I am talking about now is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted you to explain the absence of his name and now you have indicated that not all the names of the generals present were there or were recorded in your short note. Am I correct in saying that these persons you have mentioned here are the persons who made contributions or substantive contributions at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I only wrote down the names of those who contributed; therefore, I didn't even mention (redacted). That's why I couldn't recall his first name off the cuff. I still remember his nickname but not his first name. I only noted down the names of those who contributed. General Djordjevic did not. He only briefly interjected saying that General Ilic was not in attendance. I didn't write that down; I merely remembered it. And I wanted to protect that person and not mention his name in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is why I think -- I ask that that part be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- redacted from the open, public record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my mistake. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: After the meeting, did you leave with Colonel Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We were supposed to stay over a dinner. It was supposed to be a plain military dinner, but I went to see some officers who had been waiting for me at the corps and their security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I left with Colonel Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before I forget, Your Honours, could the copy of this page or pages from the notebook 052 -- sorry, 65 ter number 2862 be received in evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That, Your Honours, will be assigned P00885.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you speak to your security -- or the Pristina Corps security operative, Colonel Stojanovic, about the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I did while we were going back, since as I said I was taken by surprise by that meeting I asked him what it was. He said, Well, it's a Joint Command. It was formed back in 1998. When I asked him who were its members and who attended meetings, I first and foremost wanted to know about General Dimitrijevic, who was the head of administration. At that point he told me that initially it was Mr. Minic who attended, then Sainovic, and that during a longer period the head of the state security sector, Mr. Jovica Stanisic was there. He said that Dimitrijevic did not attend their meetings. As for state security, from Kosovo he said David Gajic was present since he was the key state security sector person in Kosovo. He also said that in the initial stages Colonel Stojanovic attended the meetings of what was called the Joint Command and that he drafted reports about what was discussed and he sent them to the security administration --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I guess I'm going too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He also said that in the initial stages -- I'm reading the record to you. He also said that in the initial stages Colonel Stojanovic attended the meetings. Is that what you intended to say?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. He also said that he drafted reports about the matters discussed and sent them to General Dimitrijevic to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who is speaking here? Who told you this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I take it that you are saying that he also said that at the initial stages he himself attended the meetings of what was called the Joint Command and that he drafted reports?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What you say is correct. He didn't keep the minutes, but he simply drew reports to be sent to the security administration chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is completely clear and unambiguous. I believe my learned friend's interpretations are unnecessary and wrong. I think it should be left to the witness to provide answers which is precisely what he's doing clearly and concisely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did he -- before I get to that, you mentioned General Dimitrijevic. What was General Dimitrijevic's post in 1998 going into 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: General Dimitrijevic was the head of the security administration from 1993 until January 1999, so in 1998 he was head of the security administration of the General Staff in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I take it General Farkas succeeded him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he succeeded him as he received that post from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did Mr. -- sorry, did Colonel Stojanovic tell you who were the -- who, if anybody, were the attendees of the Joint Command meetings from the MUP or from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: He did not tell me who the MUP attendees were; but I also already stated very clearly, he mentioned David Gajic from the state security sector, he mentioned Jovica Stanovic [as interpreted] who was head of state security sector, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Minic. I'm not sure about a person by the name of Vlatkovic, somebody from the PS [as interpreted], some of the officials, but he did not mention any officials from the MUP public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. He mentioned Jovica Stanisic, is that the correct name?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said a Vlatkovic from the PS. What is the PS?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anybody by the name of Vlajkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness said SPS not PS; it did not enter the transcript correctly. Mr. Stamp may try to clarify it. It's line 19, the PS is what is written down and the witness stated SPS. And I noted down an official -- a functioner from the SPS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say Vlajkovic, rather, I said Vlatkovic, but I am not sure about the family name of that person, so this is why I referred to the SPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You remained general in Kosovo for how long after the 1st of June?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I stayed there until the 7th of June. On the 8th of June, I was back in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We'll get back to Belgrade. I just wanted to know. In the course of time there, did you receive information as to exactly what was the role and function of the Joint Command in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, we no longer discussed that. It wasn't a relevant issue for me to be dealing with at the time. What I related, I omitted in that only one detail in that conversation while we were going back to the command of the Pristina Corps, Colonel Stojanovic told me that soon he was removed from attendance of the sessions of the Joint Command. He was told that there was -- that his attendance served no purpose, that corps commander was there, the army commander was in attendance. His personal assessment was that he was eliminated because he was reporting back to Belgrade on what was being deliberated there and this was the end of the story of the Joint Command when it came to our discussions and later on we never discussed it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the course of that discussion, did he mention to you what the purpose of the Joint Command was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: No, he did not. It wasn't an issue for us. It wasn't of interest to me, and this is why I did not ask questions about that. I just listened to what he had to say during that drive to Pristina Corps command, and this was the last time that we discussed this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up on screen document 65 ter number 01462.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An objection in advance. This document has nothing to do with this witness. The person who is supposed to verify this document has been placed - by the Trial Chamber's decision - placed on the list of witnesses for the Prosecution. I don't believe that this is appropriate for this document to be shown to this witness, especially I object to this document being introduced through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, what's the direction you're taking here, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would submit that the document is relevant and probative --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As long as the witness can identify the document and it's -- and give evidence as to its authenticity, it becomes admissible. What he might be able to say about the contents may be limited, but that is a matter for the Court to address. But if he can authenticate it, it is also my submission that it becomes admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you're planning to put this to the witness with a view to the witness identifying it in such a way as to justify its admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Go ahead, and we'll see whether you achieve your objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Colonel Djakovic who was formerly a member -- a senior member of the Pristina Corps in the 3rd Army in 1999?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first we have to ask the witness what Colonel Djakovic was, which post he occupied. My learned colleague reaches his own conclusions and then wants the witness to continue and follow up with his answers. This is a time when the witness was not in active service. On the 27th of April, 1999, he was reinstated. And before he answers, I would like to hear from him when was the first time he learned about this document if he -- any -- has any knowledge about this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The issue that needs to be addressed at the moment, Mr. Stamp, is that you were leading and that should not occur. You're on notice clearly about this document and these events against leading and tread carefully with the document so that we can see where you're going and whether it's justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see the document in front of you -- and perhaps I should -- if I could, with the leave of the Court, hand the witness a binder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you proceeding with your question about Colonel Djakovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was -- I intended to get back to that, but I could -- I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The admissible question is: Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know Colonel Djakovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC
utterances.text: I know a General Djakovic who early on was a security officer in a brigade in the 1970s. General Djakovic became head of the security administration after General Geza Farkas was removed from that post. At that time, June 2000, I was an advisor to the Chief of the General Staff for security. However, I continued working at the security administration to help General Djakovic to find his bearings because he had not reached that position from a position of responsibility in the security service but from the command of the 3rd Army. And that's why from June 2000 until 2001, in March when I left active service, I worked with him. I know him very well. We maintained contacts after I was pensioned off, and soon thereafter he was pensioned off as well. He at the time, received invitations to contact The Hague office in a certain capacity. He phoned me because he knew I had gone through such procedures. He told me that he kept minutes and this was his assessment why he was being contacted by The Hague office, the minutes of the meetings of the Joint Command in Pristina. I was interested in the circumstances leading to him keeping the minutes, and he says he himself suggested that for the first time he attended with General Pavkovic, seeing that nobody was taking the minutes as a soldier he said, General Pavkovic, nobody's noting down anything and General Pavkovic told him, Well, you take the minutes. So General Djakovic told me that for a time he kept the minutes of the sessions of the Joint Command. When I came here, I was shown a photocopy most probably of that -- those minutes. I know General Djakovic's handwriting because I worked with him, he signed documents that we sent, et cetera, so I can recognise his handwriting. I cannot be an expert graphologist, but from what I saw I gained an impression that this was General Djakovic's handwriting in the initial pages that I saw and the rest of the pages. So to cut a long story short, to resolve this enigma of me being asked about this -- in circumstances when in 1998 I was not in active duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, after such an answer by the witness, I do strenuously believe that this document cannot be introduced through him, irrespective of his subsequent knowledge gained in 2000, despite the fact that he is not a graphologist, and anyway that witness is going to testify here. I agree that this is a relevant piece of evidence, but not through this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We plan and we hope and anticipate that the witness will testify and the witness will deal with this document, as we hope and expect that he will. But the fact that another witness may come and is expected to come, it is my submission does not prevent an earlier witness who can authenticate a witness from doing so, and we never know what can happen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, we adjourn for the night because we have passed 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You reflect on it. If you propose tomorrow to -- in the morning to continue with your effort to tender the document. As I've indicated, proceed carefully with your questions, and we have already noted Mr. Djurdjic's objection and it will be the subject of decision at an appropriate time as you pursue the matter if that's the course you take in the morning. I'm afraid, General, we have to stop now. We have to finish at 7.00. We resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. We look forward to continue your evidence then. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of June, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 a.m.,
